analysis.one_liner: Requires billion-dollar corporations to get federal charters, seat employees on boards, and get shareholder approval for political spending.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require US companies with more than $1 billion in annual revenue to obtain a federal charter from a new Office of United States Corporations. Charter holders would have to pursue a 'general public benefit,' weigh employee and community interests alongside shareholder profits, elect at least 40% of their board from employees, restrict executive stock sales, and get approval from 75% of shareholders and directors before spending money on elections. State attorneys general could petition to revoke the charter of a corporation that repeatedly engaged in egregious illegal misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of the roughly 2,000 largest US companies, who would elect 40% of the board and gain a legal claim to be considered in corporate decisions; consumers and communities affected by corporate conduct; and shareholders, who would gain standing to sue over executives' stock sales and unsanctioned political spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees of large corporations and shareholders

how_it_helps.text: Requires every large entity—over $1 billion in gross receipts—to obtain a federal charter and to manage the company with a purpose of creating a 'general public benefit,' balancing shareholder interests against employees, suppliers, customers, communities, and the environment.

Requires that no less than two-fifths of directors of a covered corporation be elected by employees, with rules ensuring employee directors can be fired only for just cause; noncompliance draws civil penalties of $50,000–$100,000 per day and possible charter revocation.

Bars officers and directors from selling company stock for five years after acquiring it and for three years after the company buys back its own shares, with civil penalties of one to three times the value of the shares sold.

Requires approval by at least 75% of shareholders and 75% of directors before a corporation spends more than $10,000 supporting or opposing any candidate for federal, state, or local office, and lets shareholders sue to block spending that skips this step.

Lets a state attorney general petition to revoke the charter of a corporation that engaged in repeated, egregious, illegal misconduct causing significant harm and failed to fix the causes, such as firing the executives who oversaw it.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and their executives bear the direct cost: a new federal chartering regime, employee board seats with penalty exposure, restrictions on executive stock sales and stock-backed compensation, and a high bar for political spending. Some costs could reach consumers and investors generally if corporations pass along the added compliance and governance burden.

drawbacks.text: The 'general public benefit' standard is defined only as a 'material positive impact on society,' and the bill says directors need not prioritize any particular factor, which gives companies wide discretion and could make the charter obligation more symbolic than binding.

Enforcement is narrow: the corporation itself cannot be liable for failing to create a public benefit, outside beneficiaries have no standing to sue, and only shareholders holding at least 2% of a share class (or 5% of a parent) can bring a case—so most people the bill says it protects cannot actually sue to enforce it.

Critics of a federal corporate-chartering regime argue it would preempt a century of state corporate law and add litigation and compliance uncertainty for very large companies, costs that could be passed to consumers or shareholders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's strongest concrete provisions are employee board elections and the ban on executives cashing out stock right after their company buys back shares—both enforceable, specific rules. Its headline idea, a duty to create a 'general public benefit,' is vaguer and its enforcement doors are open mainly to large shareholders, so the bill would deliver less accountability to everyday people than its structure suggests. The political-spending approval requirement is easy to enforce and would sharply curtail corporate election spending, which supporters view as a feature and business groups would view as a burden on free association.

outcome.mechanism: Warren introduced the bill in January 2020 and it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Accountable Capitalism Act on January 16, 2020, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No cosponsors joined the bill from either party.
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded; the bill died in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest US corporations and their executives, who avoided a federal chartering regime, employee board seats, limits on executive stock sales, and a shareholder-approval requirement for political spending.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The largest US corporations and their executives

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

against.name: Sen. Roger Wicker
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split is recorded; the only support was one Democrat and zero cosponsors of either party, and the bill stalled in a Republican-chaired committee.

industries.industry: Large US corporations (over $1 billion in gross receipts)
industries.note: The bill would subject every very large company to a new federal charter, a public-benefit purpose, employee board elections with daily penalties for noncompliance, and charter-revocation petitions for repeated serious misconduct. Ordinary people stand to gain the accountability the bill is designed to create; large companies would bear the compliance and governance costs.

Executives and directors would be barred from selling company stock for five years and for three years after stock buybacks, with penalties of one to three times the shares' value. Buyback-linked pay and quick stock sales are a major source of executive wealth, so this provision hits a concentrated set of high-income individuals directly.

industries.industry: Corporate political spending and the campaign-advertising ecosystem
industries.note: Requiring 75% shareholder and director approval before any election-related spending over $10,000—defined to include payments to outside groups anticipated to be used for politics—would sharply reduce corporate money in elections. This constrains a concentrated interest while arguably serving shareholders and the general public alike.

industries.industry: State corporate law and incorporation jurisdictions (e.g., Delaware)
industries.note: A federal chartering regime would shift core corporate-governance rules from the states to a new federal office, displacing state law for the largest companies. Jurisdictions whose business rests on incorporation services would lose authority over the biggest entities while keeping it for everyone else.
